to secondary siblings instead. This is unintended consequences, episode 125. In one Kenyan household,
a mother accepted the new free uniforms for her younger children, and then kept those
same children home. The uniform subsidy had removed one cost, yet other fees remained. She
To use the money she no longer spent on primary uniforms to cover secondary school expenses
for an older child.
The program had been designed to increase primary attendance among poor families.
Instead, it produced a reallocation of limited household resources across different levels
of schooling.
Consider the arithmetic inside that decision.
A typical primary uniform might cost several hundred Kenyan shillings each year.
That sum, once freed, could cover a fraction of a secondary school term's examination or
activity levy, for an older sibling whose longer-term earnings prospects appeared higher
to the parents.
The younger children therefore stayed home, not because schooling lost all value.
The household's fixed budget could now stretch further by concentrating resources on the
child already closer to labor market entry.
This outcome was not visible in the first weeks after distribution.
Children simply appeared in new clothes.
It emerged later when attendance registers showed absences
that the original cost calculation had not anticipated.
Policy designers sought a practical way to raise
primary school participation in low-income areas
where clothing costs represented a meaningful barrier.
They reasoned that removing the requirement to purchase uniforms
would lower the direct price of attendance.
This change would therefore draw more children into classrooms.
At the time, enrollment gaps between richer and poorer households were well-documented.
An in-kind transfer appeared both administratively straightforward and politically acceptable.
Officials viewed uniforms as a visible, non-cash benefit that would reach the intended children
without creating opportunities for diversion that cash might invite.
The approach aligned with a broader preference for targeted material support over broader fee
reductions that might strain government budgets.
Decision makers operated with the information then available.
They expected the transfer to expand total primary schooling rather than rearrange existing
schooling choices within families.
They also noted that uniforms carried a signaling function.
Once children wore identical clothing, visible markers of poverty would diminish inside the classroom.

gains at the primary level. Distribution occurred through headteachers who

created an immediate, observable change that could be photographed and reported

registration beyond school roles, it scaled quickly once procurement contracts were

possible. This approach supported small tailoring enterprises and reduced import leakage. Skeptics

The dominant narrative centered on the success of getting children dressed for class,
rather than on whether every subsequent cost had also been addressed. Households facing multiple
school-aged children and a fixed budget treated the uniform savings as a fungible resource rather
than an earmarked gift. When primary school still required payment of other fees, some
families withdrew younger children to free up the newly available cash for secondary
school siblings. Those siblings faced higher fees, and their enrollment carried greater
long-term returns in parental eyes. Primary attendance therefore rose by less than planners
had projected. The subsidy shifted the composition of schooling rather than expanding its total
volume. Secondary enrollment increased as a direct result. The transfer had relaxed a household
liquidity constraint without altering the relative price of primary versus secondary options.
The causal chain ran through ordinary family budgeting. Parents maximized perceived returns
across all children once one cost item disappeared. Second order effects included uneven class

Third order effects appeared in altered expectations about which children would complete which levels of education.
The outcome illustrated how an in-kind benefit tied to one schooling stage could be repurposed across stages when households retained discretion over remaining expenditures.
In practice, the uniform represented only one line in a multi-line ledger, removing it did not change the total column of available shillings.
Families adjusted other lines instead, where a secondary place required an entrance or examination fee several times larger than a primary uniform, the arithmetic-favored moving resources upward.
This shift occurred even if it meant a younger child missed months or an entire year of primary instruction.
Over time, some communities observed that older girls in particular benefited from the redirective funds.
Secondary places for them carried both economic and social returns that parents weighed heavily once marginal cash appeared.
The program's designers had modeled the intervention as adding a discreet increment of primary schooling.
Households modeled it as relaxing an overall liquidity constraint across the entire portfolio of children's futures.
Once household responses became visible through attendance data and parent interviews,

supports would be needed to anchor the subsidy at the primary level.
Some districts experimented with bundling additional cost reductions, others narrowed
eligibility or added conditions that attempted to limit reallocation.
These adjustments themselves generated new administrative burdens and occasional mismatches
between rules and actual family circumstances.
The episode left a lasting recognition that in-kind transfers operate inside existing household
optimization rather than outside it.
This recognition influenced later design discussions about how narrowly targeted schooling supports
interact with multi-level family decisions.
Subsequent pilots tested whether pairing uniform distribution with simultaneous waivers on examination
or meal fees would reduce leakage to other schooling stages.

Over successive budget cycles, the conversation shifted from how many uniforms were delivered

Incentive structures always operate within the full set of constraints and opportunities
facing the recipients.
They do not operate merely at the single margin the program addresses.
Complex household budgets convert targeted subsidies into general resources whenever other
costs persist.
The measured effect on the intended outcome can therefore diverge sharply from the accounting
effect on the transferred item.
Designers therefore benefit from mapping the full portfolio of decisions families must make rather than isolating one line item.
